The issue with terms like "microaggression" is that they are defining a new category beyond the current linguistic ability. The act of it being very precise means that improper use is more frequent.

(I'm likely going to write a lot about this), but there is a difference between how FPH defines microaggression, how fat-activists define microaggression, how feminists define microaggressionand how the "social structure" (collective aggregate) defines microaggression. This is a key idea I have learned in life: The individual difference is linguistic definition is a point of contention. The study of psychology and language is psycholinguistics.

A simple example, imagine a dog right now. Will your cognitive visualization of what defines a "dog" match everyone in this thread? Of course not; which means if you were to argue about the characteristics of what defines a "dog", people would eventually get to the outer fringe of definition, for example - is a German Shepard more dog-like than a Chihuahua?

With a strict definition I expect most people on FPH will not deny "microaggression", but they instead would define it as "aggression" with a severity. Calling someone who is transgender by the wrong pronoun that they prefer has a different "aggression" compared to intentionally using the wrong pronoun to attack the person. People could see the accident as an act of microaggression, but I believe that is a harmful view to take. The word (like all words) has a larger pool of definitions than initially required which leads to miscommunication. When we use the word "car", we imagine a manual, gasoline device. In 50 years it may be a fully electric, self-driving platform on a "sidewalk". Everyone should be aware of this definition difference between for everything, not just "microaggression", and this can be a tool for discussion, even if people hold opposing values.
